questions.question: Differentiate between first‑order (relational) representations and propositional representations in terms of their ability to generalize across object identities.

options.A: First‑order representations can refer to object properties and relations, allowing generalization; propositional representations cannot.
options.B: Propositional representations can refer to object properties and relations, allowing generalization; first‑order representations cannot.
options.C: Both representations generalize equally across object identities.
options.D: Neither representation can express relations between objects.

questions.explanation:
First‑order (relational) representations refer to object properties and relations and thus generalize across object identities, whereas propositional representations lack this capability. [Page 199]

questions.question: Differentiate between forward chaining and backward chaining inference methods regarding the direction in which they apply rules.

options.A: Forward chaining starts from goals and works backward; backward chaining starts from facts and works forward.
options.B: Forward chaining starts from facts and applies rules forward; backward chaining starts from goals and works backward.
options.C: Both methods start from facts and proceed forward.
options.D: Both methods start from goals and proceed backward.

questions.explanation:
Forward chaining applies rules beginning with known facts, while backward chaining begins with a goal and seeks supporting facts. [Page 4]

questions.question: Differentiate between logic reasoning and first‑order (relational) representations concerning their suitability for deterministic versus uncertain knowledge bases.

options.A: Logic reasoning is suited for uncertain knowledge bases; first‑order representations are limited to deterministic knowledge.
options.B: Both logic reasoning and first‑order representations handle uncertain knowledge equally well.
options.C: Logic reasoning applies mainly to discrete, deterministic knowledge bases, whereas first‑order relational representations can express uncertain knowledge.
options.D: Neither approach can handle deterministic knowledge.

questions.explanation:
The context notes that logic reasoning is applicable to discrete & deterministic KBs, while first‑order relational representations are needed for uncertain, generalizing knowledge. [Page 199]

questions.question: Differentiate between STRIPS‑like rules and Markov Decision Process (MDP) transition representations in how they handle uncertainty.

options.A: STRIPS‑like rules inherently model probabilistic outcomes; MDP transitions are purely deterministic.
options.B: Both STRIPS‑like rules and MDP transitions are deterministic and do not model uncertainty.
options.C: STRIPS‑like rules are deterministic, while MDP transitions incorporate probabilistic (uncertain) effects.
options.D: MDP transitions ignore actions, whereas STRIPS‑like rules focus on actions only.

questions.explanation:
STRIPS‑like rules model deterministic state changes, whereas MDPs represent transitions probabilistically, allowing uncertainty. [Page 5]

questions.question: Differentiate between unification and resolution as inference mechanisms in first‑order logic concerning their primary function.

options.A: Unification combines multiple clauses into a single clause; resolution checks for syntactic equality of literals.
options.B: Unification finds a substitution that makes literals identical; resolution derives a new clause by eliminating complementary literals.
options.C: Both unification and resolution perform the same operation of clause elimination.
options.D: Resolution generates substitutions; unification derives new clauses.

questions.explanation: Unification computes substitutions that make literals match, while resolution uses those substitutions to eliminate complementary literals and produce a new clause. [Page 4]
